stem: Which of these calls changes the original array `arr` in place?

options.text: `arr.toSorted()`, which sorts the elements of the array
options.why: toSorted (ES2023) returns a sorted copy and leaves `arr` untouched.

options.text: `arr.slice(1)`, which drops the first element of the array
options.why: slice returns a new array with a portion of the elements; `arr` is unchanged.
sort reorders the elements in place and returns the same array reference.

options.text: `arr.concat([4])`, which adds a 4 onto the end of the array
options.why: concat builds and returns a new array; it never modifies `arr`.

explanation: The classic mutators are push, pop, shift, unshift, splice, sort, reverse, fill and copyWithin. ES2023 added copying counterparts (toSorted, toReversed, toSpliced, with) so you can stay immutable without a manual copy. Because `sort()` returns the same array, `const sorted = arr.sort()` gives you two names for one mutated array.

stem: What does `[10, 1, 5, 100].sort()` return?

options.why: That needs a numeric comparator such as `(a, b) => a - b`.
With no comparator, elements are compared as strings: "1" < "10" < "100" < "5".
sort is ascending by default, and it is not numeric without a comparator.
sort always reorders the elements; it just uses string order here.

explanation: Without a comparator, `sort` converts each element to a string and compares UTF-16 code units. "100" comes before "5" because the character "1" is less than "5". Pass `(a, b) => a - b` to sort numbers ascending.

stem: `[NaN].includes(NaN)` returns `true`, even though `[NaN].indexOf(NaN)` returns `-1`.

options.why: includes uses SameValueZero, which treats NaN as equal to NaN; indexOf uses strict equality, where NaN never matches.
The two methods use different comparisons, so they really do disagree on NaN.

explanation: `indexOf` and `lastIndexOf` compare with `===`, so they can never find NaN. `includes` (and Set and Map) use SameValueZero, which matches NaN. To find the position of NaN, use `findIndex(Number.isNaN)`.

stem: What does `Array.of(3)` return, and how does it differ from `Array(3)`?

options.text: `[3]`, while `Array(3)` makes an empty array of length 3
options.why: Array.of always treats its arguments as elements, which avoids the single-number trap.

options.text: `[ <3 empty items> ]`, exactly the same result as calling `Array(3)`
options.why: That is what `Array(3)` gives; Array.of exists precisely to avoid it.
The two are the other way round, and Array(3) has holes rather than undefined values.

options.text: `[0, 0, 0]`, because `Array.of` fills each of the new slots with zero
options.why: Nothing in either call fills slots with zero; use `Array(3).fill(0)` for that.

explanation: `Array(n)` with a single number creates a sparse array with `length` n and no elements. With any other arguments it creates an array of those elements. `Array.of(...items)` always does the second, so `Array.of(3)` is `[3]`.

options.why: Defaults apply only when the value is undefined; null is a real value.
That would need `a` to be undefined. A default does not replace null.
`b` is missing, so it is undefined and its default 2 applies.
Both halves are reversed: null is kept and the missing `b` gets its default.

explanation: Destructuring defaults (and default parameters) are used only when the value is `undefined`. `a` is `null`, so it stays `null`. `b` does not exist, so it is `undefined` and gets 2. To treat null as missing too, use `a ?? 1` after destructuring.

options.why: The Map keeps the number 1 and the string '1' as two separate keys.
Map keys keep their type; object keys are converted to strings, so `o[1]` and `o['1']` are the same key.
An object cannot hold both 1 and '1': numeric keys become the string '1'.
This reverses the real behaviour of the two structures.

explanation: Plain object keys are always strings or symbols, so the number 1 is converted to "1" and the second write overwrites the first. A Map compares keys with SameValueZero and no conversion, so `1` and `'1'` are distinct entries.

stem: `[1, 2] === [1, 2]` evaluates to `true` because both arrays contain the same elements in the same order.

options.why: Arrays are objects, and `===` on objects compares identity, not contents.
Correct: each literal creates a separate array, so the references differ.

explanation: Object equality in JavaScript is by reference. Two array literals are two different objects, so `==` and `===` both return false. To compare contents, compare lengths and elements yourself, or use a library deep-equal for nested data.

stem: What is the value of `y` after `const [x, , y] = [10, 20, 30];` runs? Type a number.
explanation: An empty slot between commas in an array pattern skips that element. `x` takes index 0 (10), index 1 is skipped, and `y` takes index 2 (30).

stem: ES2023 added copying versions of the mutating array methods. Match each copying method with the mutating operation it mirrors.
explanation: Each copying method returns a new array and leaves the original alone, which suits React state and other immutable updates. Note that `toSpliced` returns the new array, while `splice` returns the removed elements.

stem: Given `const a = [{ id: 1 }, { id: 2 }];`, which expressions produce a new array that is a shallow copy of `a`? (Choose three.)

options.why: Spread copies each element into a new array; the objects inside are shared.
slice with no arguments copies the whole array into a new one.
Array.from builds a new array from any iterable or array-like.
Assignment copies the reference, so `b` and `a` are the same array.
That creates `[a]`: a one-element array containing the original.
With a non-number argument, the constructor also creates `[a]`.

explanation: Spread, `slice()`, `Array.from()` and `concat()` all create a new array whose elements are the same values. That is a shallow copy: the objects `{ id: 1 }` and `{ id: 2 }` are shared, so mutating `copy[0].id` also changes `a[0].id`. Use `structuredClone` for a deep copy.

stem: What does `[...new Set([3, 1, 3, 2, 1])]` evaluate to?

options.text: `[1, 2, 3]`, the unique values in ascending order
options.why: A Set never sorts; it keeps insertion order.
Each value keeps the position where it was first added.
A repeated add is ignored; it doesn't move an existing value.
The Set has already dropped the duplicates before the spread runs.

explanation: A Set stores each value once and iterates in insertion order. Adding a value that is already present does nothing, so the first occurrence decides the position. `[...new Set(arr)]` is the idiomatic way to deduplicate primitive values.

stem:
What happens when this runs?

```js
const total = [].reduce((sum, n) => sum + n);
```

options.text: `total` is `0`, because an empty sum is zero
options.why: reduce doesn't know the identity of your operation; you must pass it.

options.text: `total` is `undefined`, because there is nothing to add
options.why: Without an initial value, an empty array has no first element to start from.
Reduce of an empty array with no initial value is an error.
The callback is never called at all; the error comes first.

explanation: Without an initial value, `reduce` uses the first element as the accumulator and starts from the second. An empty array has no first element, so it throws `TypeError: Reduce of empty array with no initial value`. A one-element array returns that element without calling the callback. Passing an initial value (`reduce(fn, 0)`) fixes both edge cases.

stem: A developer sorts numbers with `scores.sort((a, b) => a > b)`. What is wrong with this comparator?

options.text: It never returns a negative number, so it isn't a consistent comparator and the order is engine-dependent
options.why: Booleans become 1 or 0; sort needs negative, zero or positive.

options.text: Nothing: `true` and `false` convert to 1 and -1, which is exactly what sort expects from it
options.why: false converts to 0, not -1, so 'a comes first' is never signalled.

options.text: It sorts in descending order, because `a > b` is true whenever the larger number comes first
options.why: The problem is not the direction; the comparator is simply invalid.

options.text: It throws a TypeError, because a comparator must return a number and the engine checks it
options.why: The return value is converted with ToNumber; no type check throws.

explanation: A comparator must return a negative number when `a` should come first, a positive number when `b` should, and 0 for a tie, consistently. `a > b` returns only true or false, which become 1 or 0. The spec then calls the sort order implementation-defined, and with TimSort in V8 it often leaves the array unsorted. Use `(a, b) => a - b`.
reference: ECMAScript spec: SortCompare and consistent comparators

options.why: Setting length to 2 deleted indices 2–4; writing index 4 grows length back to 5 with holes.
Assigning to index 4 sets length to 5, not to one more than before.
Elements removed by shrinking length are gone for good; they don't come back.
Writing past the end of an array always updates its length.

explanation: Shrinking `length` deletes every element at or above the new length. Assigning `arr[4]` then sets `length` to 5, leaving indices 2 and 3 as holes, so `arr[3]` reads `undefined`. The array is now `[1, 2, <2 empty items>, 9]`.

stem: Compared with a plain object used as a dictionary, which are real advantages of `Map`? (Choose three.)

options.text: Keys can be any value, including objects and functions, matched by identity
options.why: Objects only support string and symbol keys.

options.text: `map.size` gives the entry count directly, without building an array of keys
options.why: With an object you need `Object.keys(o).length`, which is O(n).

options.text: Iteration follows insertion order for every key, including integer-like ones
options.why: Objects list integer-like keys first in ascending order.

options.text: `JSON.stringify(map)` serializes all of its entries automatically
options.why: A Map stringifies to `{}`; convert with `Object.fromEntries` or `[...map]` first.

options.text: `map.get({ id: 1 })` finds an entry that was stored under another `{ id: 1 }`
options.why: Object keys are matched by reference, so a new literal is a different key.

options.text: Entries can be read and written with dot notation such as `map.userId`
options.why: That sets an ordinary property on the Map object, not an entry.

explanation: Choose a Map for dynamic dictionaries: any key type, a cheap `size`, pure insertion-order iteration, no inherited keys like `toString`, and better performance for frequent adds and deletes. Choose an object for fixed records with known string keys and when you need JSON.

stem: What is `[1, [2, [3, [4]]]].flat(2).length`? Type a number.
explanation: `flat(2)` flattens two levels: `[1, [2, [3, [4]]]]` becomes `[1, 2, [3, [4]]]` after one level and `[1, 2, 3, [4]]` after two. That has 4 elements. `flat(Infinity)` would give `[1, 2, 3, 4]`. With no argument the depth is 1.

stem: Put the elements in the order that `['b10', 'b9', 'a2', 'a10'].sort()` returns them.
explanation: The default sort compares strings code unit by code unit. 'a10' and 'a2' tie on 'a', then '1' (code 49) is less than '2' (50), so 'a10' comes first. Likewise 'b10' comes before 'b9'. For natural ordering use `arr.sort((x, y) => x.localeCompare(y, undefined, { numeric: true }))`.

stem: `Object.groupBy(items, fn)` returns a `Map` whose keys are the values that `fn` returns.

options.why: That describes Map.groupBy. Object.groupBy returns a plain object.
Correct: it returns a null-prototype object whose keys are converted to strings or symbols.

explanation: ES2024 added two grouping functions. `Object.groupBy` returns an object with a null prototype, so keys are property keys (strings or symbols). `Map.groupBy` returns a Map, which keeps keys of any type, such as objects or numbers, without conversion.

stem: What does `Array.from({ length: 3 }, (_, i) => i * 2)` return?

options.why: Array.from reads indices 0 to 2 and passes each index to the mapper.
Array.from always fills real elements; it never produces holes.
The mapper uses the index `i`, not the undefined value, so no NaN appears.
Any object with a numeric length is a valid array-like source.

explanation: `{ length: 3 }` is an array-like with length 3 and no elements. Array.from reads each index (getting undefined) and calls the mapping function with `(value, index)`. This is the standard way to build ranges, such as `Array.from({ length: n }, (_, i) => i)`.

options.text: `rest` has no `a` or `b`, because rest copies only own properties
options.why: Inherited properties from `base` are not copied.

options.text: `rest` has no `d`, because rest skips non-enumerable properties
options.why: Object rest copies own enumerable properties only, so `rest` is `{}`.
It holds neither the inherited keys nor the non-enumerable one.
Rest creates a fresh plain object whose prototype is Object.prototype.

options.text: The destructuring throws, because `d` is not writable
options.why: Reading a property doesn't need it to be writable, and `d` isn't copied anyway.

explanation: Object rest (and object spread) copy own, enumerable properties into a new plain object. Here the only own enumerable properties are `c` (taken out by name) and nothing else, so `rest` is `{}`. The same rules explain why spreading a class instance loses its methods: they live on the prototype.

options.why: `with` returns a new array with one index replaced and leaves the original alone; negative indexes count from the end.
That would be true of `arr[arr.length - 1] = 9`, which mutates in place. `with` never mutates.
`with(-1, …)` is valid: like `at`, it treats -1 as the last index rather than a missing key.

options.text: It throws a `RangeError` because -1 is not a valid array index
options.why: `with` throws a RangeError only when the index is out of range after resolving negatives, for example `arr.with(5, 1)`.

explanation: `Array.prototype.with(index, value)` (ES2023) is the copying counterpart of `arr[index] = value`, alongside `toSorted`, `toReversed` and `toSpliced`. It accepts negative indexes like `at`, so `-1` means the last element. It returns a new array, so `arr` still ends in 3, `b` ends in 9, and they are different objects. Unlike plain assignment, an index outside the array throws a `RangeError` instead of growing the array.

stem: Match each requirement with the collection that fits it best.

prompts.text: Count how often each word appears, then list every word with its count
Drop duplicate numeric user IDs from a list
Attach computed metadata to DOM nodes without keeping removed nodes alive
Mark objects already visited during a graph walk without blocking their garbage collection

explanation: Map and Set hold strong references and can be iterated. WeakMap and WeakSet hold their object keys weakly, so an entry disappears once nothing else references the key. That is why they can't be iterated and have no `size`: their contents depend on the garbage collector.

options.why: That is the intermediate value; fromEntries turns it back into an object.
entries → map → fromEntries is the standard way to transform an object's values.

options.text: `{ apple: 2, pear: 3 }`, because entries returns a copy
options.why: The new pairs carry the doubled values, so the result changes.
fromEntries uses the first element of each pair as the key.

explanation: `Object.entries` turns an object into `[key, value]` pairs, `map` transforms the pairs, and `Object.fromEntries` builds a new object from them. `prices` is not modified. The same pipeline works for filtering keys, renaming keys, or converting a Map with `Object.fromEntries(map)`.

stem:
This file uses no semicolons. What happens when it runs?

```js
let a = 1
let b = 2
[a, b] = [b, a]
console.log(a, b)
```

options.why: Without a semicolon after `2`, the swap is never parsed as its own statement.

options.text: It logs `1 2`, because array destructuring copies values
options.why: The code never reaches the log; parsing joins the lines first.
The lines parse as `let b = 2[a, b] = [b, a]`, which reads `b` before it is initialized.

options.text: It throws a SyntaxError, because a line can't start with `[`
options.why: A line can start with `[`; that's exactly why ASI doesn't insert a semicolon here.

explanation: Automatic semicolon insertion only adds a semicolon when the next token can't continue the statement. `[` can continue it (as a property access), so the parser reads `let b = 2[a, b] = [b, a]`. Evaluating `2[a, b]` evaluates the comma expression `a, b`, which reads `b` while it is still in its temporal dead zone. In semicolon-free code, start such lines with `;`.

options.why: map keeps the array's length; it doesn't compact anything.
map skips the hole and leaves a hole at the same index in its result.
The callback never runs for the hole, so no NaN is produced.
map preserves holes; it does not fill them in.

explanation: Most ES5 array methods (forEach, map, filter, some, every, reduce) skip holes. map creates a result of the same length and simply doesn't define the skipped index, so the hole survives. `Object.keys` lists only the defined indices, '0' and '2'.
reference: MDN: Array (array methods and empty slots)

stem: Given `const a = [1, , 3];`, which of these visit the hole as `undefined` instead of skipping it? (Choose three.)

options.why: The array iterator reads every index from 0 to length − 1.
It reads every index, giving `[1, undefined, 3]` with no hole.
includes treats holes as undefined, so this returns true.
forEach skips holes, so `fn` runs only twice.
filter skips holes, so the hole never reaches the callback or the result.
indexOf skips holes and returns -1.

explanation: Holes are treated inconsistently. Older methods (forEach, map, filter, reduce, indexOf, some, every) skip them. Iteration-based features (for...of, spread, Array.from) and newer methods (includes, find, findIndex, at, toSorted) read them as undefined. Avoid sparse arrays, or normalise with `Array.from`.
reference: MDN: Array (array methods and empty slots)

options.why: Groups appear in the order first seen, and the result has no Object.prototype.
The key order is right, but the result object has a null prototype.
1 creates 'odd' first; a null-prototype object has no hasOwnProperty.

options.text: `[] 'undefined'`, because the groups live in a Map
options.why: Object.groupBy returns an object; Map.groupBy is the one that returns a Map.

explanation: `Object.groupBy` creates a group key when it first sees it, so 'odd' (from 1) comes before 'even' (from 2). Each value is an array: `{ odd: [1, 3], even: [2, 4] }`. The object has a null prototype, so keys like 'constructor' or 'toString' can't clash with inherited ones, but `g.hasOwnProperty` doesn't exist. Use `Object.hasOwn(g, 'odd')`.

Own string keys are ordered in two groups: integer-like keys first, in ascending numeric order ('1', '2'), then the other string keys in insertion order ('b', 'a', 'c'). Symbol keys come last and aren't included by Object.keys. If you need pure insertion order for keys like IDs, use a Map.

options.why: union returns a new Set; `a` is unchanged.

options.text: `[1, 2, 3] 3`, because union adds the values of `b` into `a`
options.why: The ES2025 Set methods never mutate the receiver.

options.text: `[1, 2, 2, 3] 2`, because union keeps both copies of 2
options.why: The result is a Set, so 2 appears only once.

options.text: It throws a TypeError, because union is still only a proposal
options.why: The Set methods are part of ES2025 and ship in all major engines.

explanation: ES2025 added `union`, `intersection`, `difference`, `symmetricDifference`, `isSubsetOf`, `isSupersetOf` and `isDisjointFrom` to Set. They take any set-like argument (with `size`, `has` and `keys`) and return new Sets or booleans without mutating either input. They ship in Chrome 122+, Firefox 127+, Safari 17+ and Node 22+; older targets need a polyfill.

stem: `'a👋b'.length` is 4. What is `[...'a👋b'].length`? Type a number.
explanation: String `length` counts UTF-16 code units, and the emoji U+1F44B takes two (a surrogate pair), so the length is 4. The string iterator, used by spread, for...of and Array.from, yields whole code points, so the result is `['a', '👋', 'b']` with 3 elements. Grapheme clusters such as flags or skin-tone emoji need `Intl.Segmenter`.

options.why: Spread needs an iterable; an object with a length isn't one.

options.text: `x` is `['a', 'b']`, then the spread throws a TypeError
options.why: Array.from accepts array-likes; spread only accepts iterables.

options.text: Both lines throw, because the object is not an array
options.why: Array.from was designed to handle array-likes such as `arguments` and NodeLists.
This reverses the two behaviours.

explanation: An array-like has a `length` and indexed properties. An iterable has a `[Symbol.iterator]` method. Array.from checks for an iterator first and falls back to array-like reading. Array spread uses only the iterator, so a plain object throws 'arrayLike is not iterable'. Real arrays, strings, Maps, Sets, NodeLists and `arguments` are both.

stem: For an array of n elements in a typical engine, which operations take time proportional to n? (Choose two.)

options.why: Removing the first element moves every remaining element down one index.
includes scans elements one by one until it finds a match.
Removing the last element needs no re-indexing, so it is O(1).
Appending is amortized O(1); the engine grows capacity in chunks.
Indexed access on a dense array is O(1).

options.text: `set.has(x)` on a Set built from the array
options.why: Set lookups are hash-based, O(1) on average.

explanation: Using `shift` in a loop to process a queue makes the loop O(n²); use an index pointer or a deque instead. Likewise `arr.includes` inside a loop over another array is O(n × m); build a Set once for O(1) lookups. Engines may optimise specific cases, but you can't rely on it.
reference: V8 blog: Elements kinds; MDN: Set.prototype.has()

stem: Under ES2023 and later, which of these can be used as keys in a `WeakMap`? (Choose two.)

options.why: Objects are the classic weak key, held without preventing collection.
ES2023 allows non-registered symbols as weak keys, because they can be collected.
Primitives like strings can be recreated at any time, so they are rejected with a TypeError.
Registered symbols live forever in the global registry, so they are not allowed.
Numbers are primitives and are rejected as weak keys.

explanation: A weak key must be something with a unique identity that can be garbage-collected: objects and, since ES2023, symbols that are not in the global registry. Strings, numbers and registered symbols could be recreated at any time, so 'is it still reachable?' has no meaning for them and `set` throws a TypeError.
reference: MDN: WeakMap (keys); TC39 Symbols as WeakMap keys

options.text: `'Ada' 1`, because spread copies nested objects too
options.why: Spread is shallow; `next.user` is the same object as `state.user`.
`user` is shared, so the edit shows in `state`; `tags` was replaced with a new array.

options.text: `'Grace' 2`, because both nested values are shared
options.why: `tags` was given a new array, so `state.tags` still has one element.

options.text: `'Ada' 2`, because only arrays are shared by reference
options.why: Arrays and objects are both shared by a shallow copy.

explanation: Object spread copies top-level properties, so nested objects are shared. `tags` was explicitly replaced, which is correct immutable updating. `user` was not, so mutating `next.user` also mutates `state.user`, the classic bug behind React state that 'doesn't update'. Copy every level you change: `{ ...state, user: { ...state.user, name: 'Grace' } }`.
reference: React docs: Updating objects in state

stem: Match each expression on an empty array with its result.
explanation: `every` on an empty array is vacuously true and `some` is false, which matches logic's 'for all' and 'there exists'. `Math.max()` with no arguments returns -Infinity, the identity for max. reduce without an initial value has nothing to start from and throws. Guard empty inputs explicitly in validation code.

options.text: `counts` is `1`, because each assignment evaluates to the number it stored
options.why: That is the sloppy-mode outcome; modules are strict, where the second call throws.

options.text: A TypeError on the second call
options.why: `acc` is now the number 1, and strict code can't create a property on a number.

options.text: `counts` is `2`, the number of distinct keys
options.why: Nothing in the callback counts keys; it returns the value just assigned.

explanation: An assignment expression evaluates to the assigned value. The first call returns 1, so `acc` becomes the number 1 on the second call. `1['b'] = ...` tries to create a property on a primitive. Sloppy scripts silently ignore that (ending with `counts === 1`), but modules are strict, so it throws 'Cannot create property 'b' on number '1''. Return the accumulator: `(acc[k] = (acc[k] || 0) + 1, acc)`, or use a block body.

stem: Why is `arr.sort(() => Math.random() - 0.5)` a poor way to shuffle an array?

options.text: It's fine: every comparison is a coin flip, which makes all n! orders equally likely
options.why: Real sort algorithms don't make one independent comparison per pair, so the coin flips don't produce uniform orders.

options.text: The comparator is inconsistent, so the result is implementation-defined and biased
options.why: Some orders come out far more often; Fisher–Yates gives each order equal odds.

options.text: It throws a RangeError in modern engines, which reject comparators that aren't deterministic
options.why: No engine detects or rejects random comparators; the code runs and returns a biased order.

options.text: It only goes wrong for arrays over 10 elements, where V8 changes its sort algorithm
options.why: V8 has used TimSort for every size since 2018, and the bias exists for small arrays too.

explanation: The spec requires a consistent comparator: the same pair must always compare the same way. A random comparator breaks that, so the order is implementation-defined. In practice, insertion-based sorts leave elements near their starting positions far more often than chance. Fisher–Yates walks from the end and swaps each element with a random earlier-or-equal index, giving each of the n! orders probability 1/n!.

options.why: No array can be that long; the maximum length is 2³² − 1.
2³² − 1 is not a valid array index, so it is stored as an ordinary property.
That would be true for index 2³² − 2, the largest real array index.
That error comes from assigning `length` directly, not from writing this key.

explanation: Array indices are integers from 0 to 2³² − 2, because `length` must fit in 2³² − 1. The key '4294967295' is therefore an ordinary string property. It doesn't affect `length`, though Object.keys still lists it. Writing `a[2 ** 32 - 2]` would set length to 4294967295, the maximum.
reference: ECMAScript spec: Array exotic objects (array index)

options.text: `4 false true`, because holes are sorted before undefined
options.why: The order is the other way round: undefined values first, then holes.

options.text: `3 true false`, because sort removes the hole from the array
options.why: sort never changes the length; the hole moves to the end.
The result is `[1, 3, undefined, <empty>]`.

options.text: `4 true true`, because sort turns the hole into undefined
options.why: That is toSorted's behaviour; sort keeps the hole.

explanation: sort collects the existing elements (skipping holes): `[3, undefined, 1]`. undefined always sorts to the end and is never passed to the comparator, giving `[1, 3, undefined]`. These are written back to indices 0–2, and the remaining index 3 is deleted, so the hole ends up last. `toSorted()` instead reads holes as undefined, returning `[1, 3, undefined, undefined]`.

stem: What does `new Uint8Array([256, 257, -1, 3.9])` contain?

options.why: Values are truncated toward zero and then wrapped modulo 256.

options.text: `[255, 255, 0, 4]`, with every value clamped to the 0–255 range
options.why: Clamping and rounding are what Uint8ClampedArray does, not Uint8Array.

options.text: A RangeError, because 256, 257 and -1 don't fit into a single byte
options.why: Typed arrays never throw on out-of-range values; they convert them.
Each element is one unsigned byte, so it can only hold integers 0 to 255.

explanation: Uint8Array converts with ToUint8: truncate toward zero, then take the value modulo 2⁸. 256 → 0, 257 → 1, -1 → 255, 3.9 → 3. Uint8ClampedArray (used by canvas ImageData) clamps to 0–255 and rounds half to even instead, so `[300, -5, 2.5]` becomes `[255, 0, 2]`.

options.text: `0 1`, because the most significant byte is stored first
options.why: That is big-endian order, which almost no hardware running JavaScript uses.

options.text: `1 0` on little-endian hardware, which is nearly every device
options.why: Typed arrays use the platform's byte order; the low byte comes first.

options.text: `1 1`, because each view holds its own separate copy of the data

options.text: A TypeError, because two typed arrays can't share one buffer
options.why: Sharing a buffer between views is exactly what ArrayBuffer is for.

explanation: Typed array views over one ArrayBuffer read and write the same bytes. Multi-byte views use the platform's native byte order, which is little-endian on x86 and ARM, so the 32-bit value 1 is stored as bytes 01 00 00 00. For file formats and network protocols with a fixed byte order, use `DataView` with its explicit `littleEndian` argument.

stem: Which statements are true? (Choose three.)

options.why: Set uses SameValueZero, which treats NaN as equal to itself.
Map keys also use SameValueZero, so NaN works as a key.
SameValueZero treats 0 and -0 as the same value.
includes uses SameValueZero, so this is true and the statement is false.
indexOf uses ===, so it returns -1.
A Set normalises -0 to +0 when it is added, so the value read back is +0.

explanation: Collections use SameValueZero: NaN equals NaN, and 0 equals -0. Sets and Maps go one step further and store -0 as +0, so the sign is lost. `===` differs on NaN, and only `Object.is` (SameValue) distinguishes 0 from -0. Knowing which comparison each API uses explains every one of these results.

stem: Which statements about the ES2023 copying array methods are true? (Choose two.)

options.why: with accepts negative indices counted from the end, like `at`.
The copying methods read holes as undefined, so the copy is dense.
with never grows the array; an out-of-range index throws a RangeError.

options.text: `arr.toReversed()` reverses `arr` in place and returns it
options.why: toReversed returns a new array and leaves `arr` unchanged.
toSpliced returns the new array `[2, 3]`; only splice returns removed elements.

explanation: `toSorted`, `toReversed`, `toSpliced` and `with` always return a new, dense array of the same kind. Unlike assigning `arr[i] = v`, `with(i, v)` validates the index and throws a RangeError when it is out of range, which catches off-by-one bugs early.

stem: Which statements about `WeakRef` and `FinalizationRegistry` are guaranteed by the language? (Choose two.)

options.text: `ref.deref()` returns the target, or `undefined` once the target has been collected
options.why: That is the whole contract: you get the object or nothing.

options.text: A FinalizationRegistry cleanup callback might never run, for example if the page closes first
options.why: The spec makes no promise that cleanup runs at all.

options.text: `deref()` starts returning `undefined` as soon as the last strong reference is dropped
options.why: Collection happens whenever the engine decides, possibly much later or never.

options.text: Cleanup callbacks run synchronously, at the moment the target is collected
options.why: They are queued as separate tasks and run later, if at all.

options.text: An object returned by `deref()` can be collected before the current job finishes
options.why: The engine keeps a deref'd target alive until the end of the current synchronous job.

explanation: WeakRef and FinalizationRegistry expose garbage collection, which is non-deterministic, so the spec promises very little. The one useful guarantee is that a target you deref'd stays alive for the rest of the current job, so two derefs in one turn agree. Use them only for caches and resource-leak backstops, never for program logic that must run.
reference: MDN: WeakRef (notes on WeakRefs); TC39 WeakRefs proposal

explanation: Set iteration is live. Deleting 'b' removes it from its slot, and adding it again appends it at the end, after 'c'. The iterator then continues: it skips the emptied slot, visits 'c', and finally visits the re-added 'b'. Maps behave the same way, so deleting and re-setting a key moves it to the end. That is how simple LRU caches built on Map work.
